stem: Two nuclei have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. What describes their relationship?
options: They are isotopes of the same element
They are isobars of different elements
They have the same nucleon number
They must have the same half-life
explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number (number of protons) but different neutron numbers.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A nucleus of thorium-232 (proton number 90) emits an alpha particle. What is the nucleon number and proton number of the daughter nucleus?
explanation: Alpha emission removes two protons and two neutrons, reducing nucleon number by 4 and proton number by 2.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A neutron undergoes beta-minus decay. Which pair of particles is emitted in addition to a proton?
options: A positron and an electron antineutrino
A positron and an electron neutrino
An electron and an electron antineutrino
An electron and an electron neutrino
explanation: n → p + e⁻ + electron antineutrino. The antineutrino ensures lepton number is conserved.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A proton in a nucleus changes into a neutron by beta-plus decay. Which particles are emitted?
options: An electron and an electron antineutrino
An electron and an electron neutrino
A positron and an electron antineutrino
A positron and an electron neutrino
explanation: Beta-plus decay is p → n + e⁺ + electron neutrino. The positron has lepton number −1, balanced by a neutrino.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: An excited nucleus emits a gamma-ray photon. Which change occurs in its nucleon number and proton number?
explanation: Gamma radiation carries energy but no nucleons and no electric charge, so A and Z are unchanged.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: Which ranking of alpha, beta and gamma radiation is in order of increasing typical penetration through matter?
explanation: Alpha is typically stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta penetrates farther; gamma generally requires substantial shielding.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: An isotope is used as a tracer to detect leaks in a buried water pipe. Which property is most important for radiation to be detected above ground?
options: A half-life of several thousand years
Strong penetration through pipe and soil
Very high ionising power in water
explanation: The emitted radiation must pass through pipe material and surrounding soil to reach a detector. A practical tracer must also have a suitable half-life.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A radioactive sample has half-life 12 hours. What fraction of its original undecayed nuclei remain after 36 hours?
explanation: 36/12=3 half-lives, so the remaining fraction is (1/2)³=1/8.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: The net activity of a radioactive sample is initially 960 Bq. Its half-life is 8 minutes. What is its net activity after 24 minutes?
explanation: Three half-lives elapse; 960 / 2³ = 120 Bq.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A detector records 440 counts per minute from a radioactive source and background combined. The background count rate is 40 counts per minute. If the source has a half-life of 10 minutes, what total count rate is expected after 20 minutes?
explanation: Initial source-only rate = 440−40=400 counts/min. After two half-lives it is 100, then adding background gives 140 counts/min.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: Two pure radioactive sources P and Q have identical half-lives. Initially P has three times the activity of Q. After four half-lives, what is the ratio of the activity of P to that of Q?
explanation: Both activities are multiplied by (1/2)⁴, so their ratio remains 3.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A sketch of binding energy per nucleon versus nucleon number is shown. What does the height of the curve indicate about nuclei near its maximum?
options: They have the largest nuclear radius
Their nucleons are relatively strongly bound
explanation: The higher binding energy per nucleon indicates more energy is needed on average to separate each nucleon.
diagramAlt: Binding energy per nucleon rises sharply for light nuclei, peaks near nucleon number 56, then decreases gradually.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: The mass of a bound nucleus is less than the total mass of its separated protons and neutrons. What does this difference represent?
options: Energy released during nucleus formation divided by c²
A violation of conservation of mass-energy
The kinetic energy of a stationary nucleus
The rest mass of electrons removed from the atom
explanation: The mass defect corresponds to the binding energy through E = Δmc².
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: The total binding energy of a nucleus is 84 MeV and it contains 12 nucleons. What is the binding energy per nucleon?
explanation: 84 MeV divided by 12 nucleons gives 7 MeV per nucleon.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: An alpha particle, a beta-minus particle and a gamma photon have equal initial kinetic energies. Which generally produces the densest ionisation along its track in air?
explanation: An alpha particle is massive and doubly charged, producing dense ionisation over a short range.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A sample contains 5.0 × 10¹¹ radioactive nuclei. Its decay constant is 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. What is its activity?
explanation: A = λN = (2.0×10⁻⁵)(5.0×10¹¹)=1.0×10⁷ decays per second.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: The graph shows the activity of a pure radioactive source. What is the approximate decay constant in h⁻¹?
explanation: Activity halves from 160 kBq to 80 kBq in 4.0 h, so λ=ln2/4≈0.173 h⁻¹.
diagramAlt: Exponentially decreasing activity from 160 kBq at t=0 to 80 kBq at 4 h.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A radioactive source has initial activity 800 Bq and decay constant 0.30 day⁻¹. What is its activity after 5.0 days?
explanation: A=A₀e⁻λt=800 e⁻¹⋅⁵ ≈179 Bq. This requires the continuous decay law for an arbitrary time interval.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: For radioactive decay with decay constant λ, under what condition is λΔt approximately equal to the probability that one nucleus decays in a time interval Δt?
options: The activity of the sample is zero
The sample contains exactly one nucleus
explanation: The exact decay probability in the interval is 1−e⁻λΔt; for λΔt ≪ 1 it is approximately λΔt.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A nucleus emits beta-minus radiation. Its emitted electrons have a continuous range of energies. What explains the range?
options: The available energy is shared variably with an antineutrino
Every beta electron starts with exactly zero kinetic energy
The electron loses all its energy inside the nucleus
explanation: The decay energy is distributed among the beta electron, antineutrino and recoiling daughter, so the beta spectrum is continuous.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: An excited nucleus emits gamma radiation of distinct photon energies. What is supported by the discrete gamma-ray spectrum?
options: Every nucleus has the same mass
The nucleus is held together by gravity
explanation: Each spectral line corresponds to a particular energy difference between discrete nuclear states.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: Which observation provides evidence that the strong nuclear force is short-range?
options: Very large nuclei have much higher binding energy per nucleon than iron
The nuclear force acts equally between all particles at any separation
Binding energy per nucleon is approximately constant across many nuclei with A above about 60
All isotopes have the same half-life
explanation: The saturation of binding energy per nucleon is consistent with each nucleon interacting strongly mainly with nearby nucleons.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: For many light stable nuclei, the ratio of neutrons to protons is close to one. For heavy stable nuclei, this ratio is generally greater than one. What best explains this?
options: The strong force becomes long-range in heavier nuclei
Additional neutrons help provide nuclear attraction without increasing proton–proton repulsion
explanation: As proton number increases, proton–proton electrostatic repulsion increases, so additional neutrons help stability without adding electric repulsion.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.

stem: A source initially contains 3.0 × 10¹² radioactive nuclei with a half-life of 6.0 hours. Approximately how many nuclei will remain after 9.0 hours?
explanation: N=N₀2⁻ᵗ⁄ᵀ =3.0×10¹² ×2⁻¹⋅⁵≈1.06×10¹². An arbitrary time interval requires exponential decay.
sourceNote: Original question aligned to IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025), E.3. Uploaded E.3 exam questions used for scope and difficulty calibration, not reproduced.
